intro:
These exercises take the borrowing and lifetime rules from Chapter 4 and push them into struct design, where they stop being a borrow-checker formality and become a public data-modeling decision. Every struct in a service is implicitly a policy statement: a borrowed field declares "I am a temporary lens over data someone else owns," and an owned field declares "I am a value the rest of the system may keep, move, queue, test, and reason about on its own." The work here is learning to classify each struct into one of those two roles deliberately, and to recognize the contagion that follows when a single reference field forces a lifetime parameter onto everything that touches the type.

The set builds toward a single durable habit: keep borrowed views local to parsing and validation, convert to owned forms at the first storage, queue, retry, or thread boundary, and reach for Box, Rc, and Arc only when the ownership-count and thread questions genuinely call for them. The lab and the owned-buffer exercises drill the most Rust-native pattern in this space — own the buffer once, slice borrowed views from &self on demand — while the pointer and refactoring exercises make you commit to a representation that Rust can move and store without lifetime baggage.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose owned versus borrowed fields for two domain objects
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The two structs have different jobs, so they should have different field shapes. RouteMatchView exists only during request parsing, while the request buffer is still alive and pinned in scope. It is a temporary lens over that buffer, so its fields should borrow directly from it: the matched path, the route pattern, and any captured path parameters are all slices into the incoming bytes. Borrowing here is cheap and the upstream owner is obvious and nearby — the buffer the parser is reading from — so the lifetime relationship is local and easy to name. RouteMatchView<'a> never escapes the parse function, so its lifetime parameter never spreads anywhere.

StoredRouteMatch is the opposite. It outlives the parse step on purpose: it goes into a metrics aggregator, a retry queue, and possibly a persistence layer, all of which run after the request buffer has been recycled or dropped. Every field that must survive that boundary has to be owned — the route id and matched path as String (or an interned id), captured parameters as owned Strings, the timestamp and status as plain Copy values. If StoredRouteMatch borrowed from the buffer, it could not sit in a Vec, a channel, or a cache without dragging the buffer's lifetime along, and it would be impossible to hold across an await point or send to another thread.

The concrete reason the two structs should not share field types: a borrowed &'a str ties the holder to the buffer's lifetime, but the stored record's whole reason to exist is to be independent of that buffer. Forcing one struct to serve both jobs means either the view pays for allocations it does not need during the hot parse path, or the stored record inherits a lifetime parameter that contaminates the metrics, retry, and persistence code downstream. The tradeoff is explicit: StoredRouteMatch pays a handful of allocations at the conversion boundary to buy lifetime independence for everything after it. That allocation is almost always worth it, because the alternative is a lifetime-coupled object graph that cannot be queued, retried, or tested in isolation.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The view borrows from the buffer; into_stored is the single allocation boundary that produces an owned, queueable record.
criteria: RouteMatchView borrows only from the request buffer, whose ownership is obvious and lexically nearby during parsing.
StoredRouteMatch owns every field that must survive past the parse step into metrics, retries, and persistence.
The stated tradeoff: a few allocations at into_stored buy lifetime independence, versus a lifetime-coupled graph that cannot be queued or tested.

exerciseSolutions.title: Explain the lifetime coupling in a borrowed-field struct
exerciseSolutions.solution:
In struct HeaderView<'a> { name: &'a str, value: &'a str }, the bytes behind name and value are owned by something outside the struct — typically the request buffer or response buffer the parser is scanning. HeaderView holds no String, no Vec, no heap allocation of its own; both fields are slices that point into memory the struct does not own. The struct is a window onto that memory, not a copy of it.

The struct needs the lifetime parameter <'a> because it stores references, and a reference is only meaningful relative to the validity of the thing it points at. The compiler cannot type-check HeaderView in isolation; it has to connect the references inside the struct to the owner outside it. <'a> is that connection. Operationally it says: a HeaderView<'a> is valid only as long as the borrow 'a is valid, and the compiler will refuse to let any HeaderView outlive the buffer its slices came from. It is a relationship marker between this struct and an external owner.

What <'a> does not say is just as important. It is not a retention policy and it does not extend storage lifetime. Writing HeaderView<'a> does not make the bytes live longer; it only records that the struct depends on bytes that live for at least 'a. The struct constrains reference validity; it does not own or prolong anything. That is why this design is comfortable in parsing code: the buffer is right there on the stack, the views are produced and consumed inside the same function, and 'a stays local and short. It becomes awkward in caches and queues for the mirror-image reason — a cache entry or a queued message is supposed to outlive the request that produced it, but a HeaderView is structurally forbidden from outliving its buffer. To store one, you would have to keep the entire originating buffer alive for as long as the cache entry lives, or thread 'a through the cache type itself, which spreads the lifetime parameter across the whole storage layer. At that point you want an owned Header { name: String, value: String } instead.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: HeaderView is a borrowed lens valid only within the buffer's lifetime; storing it long-term requires the owned Header form.
criteria: States that name and value borrow from an external owner (the buffer), so the struct cannot outlive that owner.
Explains <'a> constrains reference validity and does not extend or prolong storage lifetime.
Names parsing as the good fit and caches/queues as the burdensome case where an owned Header is needed.

exerciseSolutions.title: Build a struct that owns a buffer and exposes read-only views safely
exerciseSolutions.solution:
AuditLine owns the raw line as a single String field and exposes level(&self) -> &str, which slices the text before the first colon out of that owned buffer on demand. This is the own-the-buffer, borrow-the-view pattern that the chapter's first example demonstrates with LogLine. The struct manages the lifetime of the data; callers receive a cheap, read-only &str that is derived from &self at call time rather than stored.

The key move is that level does not create a new owned String and does not store a second field. It returns a slice whose lifetime is tied to the &self borrow, so the borrow lives and dies with each call. Because nothing inside the struct points back at the raw field, AuditLine has no lifetime parameter, no self-reference, and no aliasing — it is an ordinary movable value. self.raw.split(':').next() yields everything up to the first colon ("WARN" for "WARN: cache miss"), and unwrap_or("UNKNOWN") supplies a fallback for a line with no colon. split alone, not split_whitespace, gives "WARN" with no trailing space because the colon is the delimiter.

The constructor must actually store the data: the starter code's bug is raw: String::new(), which throws the argument away and leaves an empty buffer. Replacing it with raw.to_string() copies the input into the owned field once. After that, the struct can be sliced as many times as needed without any further allocation, which is exactly why this pattern dominates log parsing, protocol headers, and message frames — own once, slice many times.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: raw.to_string() owns the line once; level returns a &str sliced from &self, with no stored self-reference.
criteria: raw is stored as an owned String, copied in via raw.to_string().
level returns a borrowed &str sliced from &self, not a stored field and not a new allocation.
Running it prints exactly 'level = WARN' then 'raw = WARN: cache miss', matching the required output.

exerciseSolutions.title: Refactor a self-referential design into stable indices
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The shape struct ParsedLine<'a> { raw: String, first: &'a str } is the classic self-referential trap. The intent is for first to point into raw, but the type cannot say that: 'a is supplied by the caller, not by the struct's own raw field, and even if it were, filling first means borrowing self.raw while moving raw into the same value. Those two operations conflict, and there is no safe way to express "borrow from my own field" because moving the struct would invalidate the internal pointer. So the redesign must remove the self-reference entirely.

The practical repair, matching the chapter's stable-indices example, is to store the first token as a byte range — a (start, end) offset pair, or a Range<usize> — instead of a reference. The struct keeps owning raw and adds first: Range<usize> (a value with no lifetime parameter, cheap to clone). The accessor first(&self) -> &str then reconstructs the borrowed view at call time by slicing &self.raw[self.first.clone()]. The crucial property is that the borrow originates from &self at call time, so its lifetime is the call's borrow, not a stored 'a. The struct itself has no lifetime parameter, moves freely, and can sit in a Vec, a cache, or a channel.

Offsets are preferred over a typed token id here because for recovering a single substring, offsets are the simplest thing that works and they carry no extra machinery. A typed token id makes sense only when you have an interner or token table the id indexes into; here there is none, so an id would just add indirection. The one rule the design must respect is that the stored offsets are only valid as long as raw is not mutated in a way that shifts byte positions. If the buffer can be truncated, spliced, or re-tokenized, the offsets become stale exactly the way a raw pointer would dangle. So either treat raw as immutable after construction, or recompute the offsets whenever the buffer changes — the indexing metadata and the buffer have to be kept in agreement.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: first is a Range<usize>, not a self-reference; the accessor slices it from the owned buffer per call, so the struct stays movable.
criteria: The redesign removes the &'a str self-reference completely; ParsedLine has no lifetime parameter.
It stores stable metadata — a Range<usize> byte-offset pair — instead of a reference.
The accessor first(&self) reconstructs &str by slicing the owned buffer at call time, borrowing from &self.
Notes that mutating raw can invalidate the offsets, so the buffer must stay immutable or the ranges must be recomputed.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose Box, Rc, or Arc intentionally
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Each pointer answers an ownership-count and thread question, not a mutability question, so the right move is to ask "how many owners?" and "which threads?" before naming the type. The recursive AST node owned by one parent is a single-owner case that needs indirection only because a struct cannot contain itself by value — the size would be infinite. Box<T> is exactly the right tool: it provides heap indirection without changing the ownership count. There is one owner, the parent, and Box gives a stable single-owner pointer that breaks the recursive size cycle. No reference counting is involved because nothing is shared.

The read-mostly UI template shared inside one thread has more than one owner — several parts of the UI hold the same template — but they all live on the same thread. Rc<T> fits: it is shared ownership with a non-atomic reference count, cheap to clone because incrementing the count is a plain integer add. Rc is wrong at a thread boundary precisely because its count is non-atomic; two threads cloning or dropping it concurrently would race on that counter and corrupt it, so Rc is !Send and !Sync and the compiler will not let it cross a thread. That is a feature, not a limitation — it makes the cheaper non-atomic count safe to use within one thread.

The schema object shared across worker threads needs Arc<T>. Arc is the same shared-ownership idea as Rc but with an atomic reference count, so cloning and dropping from multiple threads is safe. The extra truth that must hold before Arc is enough: T itself must be thread-safe. Arc<T> is Send and Sync only when T is Sync (and Send), so Arc makes the reference count safe to share, but it does nothing about the interior. If the schema needs to be mutated across threads, Arc alone is not enough — you need Arc<Mutex<T>> or Arc<RwLock<T>> to make the contents safely shareable. For a read-only schema that is fine as-is, Arc<Schema> is sufficient.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Box for single-owner recursion, Rc for same-thread sharing, Arc for cross-thread sharing where the inner type stays thread-safe.
criteria: Box<T> is chosen for the recursive single-owner AST node, giving indirection without changing the owner count.
Rc<T> is chosen for the same-thread shared UI template, and its non-atomic count is identified as why it cannot cross threads.
Arc<T> is chosen for the cross-thread schema, with the explicit note that T must remain thread-safe (and Arc<Mutex<T>> is needed for shared mutation).

exerciseSolutions.title: Design long-lived service structs without over-lifetime-parameterization
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The pipeline socket bytes -> parse headers -> build Event -> enqueue -> retry -> persist has exactly one natural region for borrowed views and a clear boundary past which everything must be owned. The types that exist only inside parsing or validation are the view types: a HeaderView<'a> and a RequestLineView<'a> that slice directly into the socket buffer, plus any transient validation result that references those slices. These never leave the parse-and-validate function. Their lifetime parameter stays local because nothing downstream holds them, so the contagion the chapter warns about never starts. Borrowing here is the right call — it is the hot path, the buffer is alive and nearby, and we avoid allocating for data we may reject during validation.

Event becomes fully owned at the enqueue boundary, and that is the single most important decision in the design. The queue is where the data stops being a lens over the socket buffer and becomes a value the system keeps: the buffer will be recycled for the next request long before the retry and persist stages run, and a queued or retried item may also cross an await point or a thread. So the conversion from borrowed views to an owned Event { method: String, path: String, headers: Vec<(String, String)>, body: Vec<u8>, ... } happens right before enqueue. Queues and retries are ownership boundaries; anything that survives past the input buffer should stop borrowing from it. Every type downstream of the queue — the retry envelope, the persistence record — is plain owned data with no lifetime parameter, which is what keeps the bulk of the service from becoming Thing<'a>.

Arc<T> is semantically real in exactly one place here: shared, read-only configuration or schema that the parse, validation, and persistence stages all reference and that may be read from worker threads — for example Arc<Schema> or Arc<RouteTable>. There it encodes genuine many-owner, cross-thread sharing. Arc would merely hide unclear ownership if it were wrapped around the Event itself just to dodge a move or a clone; an Event has one logical owner as it flows through the pipeline, so Arc<Event> would substitute reference counting for a clear handoff and obscure who is responsible for it. The tradeoff I accept explicitly: I pay the allocations to deep-copy the borrowed views into an owned Event at the enqueue boundary. That is real cost on every request, but it buys lifetime independence for the entire post-queue half of the system — retry, persistence, metrics, and tests all operate on a self-contained value with no external lifetime baggage, no Thing<'a> contagion, and no socket buffer pinned alive longer than it should be.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Borrowed views stay inside parsing; build_event is the one allocation boundary; Arc<Schema> models real shared read-only state, not Event itself.
criteria: Borrowed HeaderView/RequestLineView types are confined to parsing and validation, keeping their lifetimes local.
Event is converted to fully owned form at the enqueue boundary, before retry and persistence run.
Arc is justified only for genuinely shared read-only schema/config, and rejected for Event where it would hide a clear single-owner handoff.
The accepted tradeoff is the per-request allocation at build_event, bought in exchange for keeping the post-queue half of the system free of lifetime parameters.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
level = WARN
raw = WARN: cache miss
labSolution.explanation:
The starter code had two stubs. The constructor stored String::new(), discarding the argument and leaving an empty buffer, and level() returned the hardcoded "UNKNOWN". The fix is the own-the-buffer, borrow-the-view pattern: new copies the input into the owned raw field with raw.to_string(), so AuditLine holds the whole line, and level slices a read-only view out of that owned field on demand.

Inside level, self.raw.split(':') splits "WARN: cache miss" on the colon, and next() takes the first piece, "WARN". The unwrap_or("UNKNOWN") fallback only matters for a line with no colon. The returned &str borrows from &self, so its lifetime is the call's borrow rather than a stored field — there is no self-reference and no lifetime parameter on the struct, which keeps AuditLine an ordinary movable value.

main prints level = WARN from line.level() and raw = WARN: cache miss from line.raw, because the constructor now actually owns the original line. That produces exactly the two expected output lines.

reviewAnswers.question: When is a borrowed-field struct a strong design, and when is it a maintenance smell?
reviewAnswers.answer: A borrowed-field struct is a strong design when it is a short-lived lens over data an obvious, nearby owner holds — for example header or request-line views produced and consumed inside a single parse function, where the lifetime stays local and the borrow is cheap. It becomes a maintenance smell when the struct is meant to be stored, queued, retried, cached, sent across threads, or held across an await point, because then it is structurally forbidden from outliving the buffer it borrows from. The tell is the moment you find yourself threading its lifetime parameter through storage types, channels, or test fixtures; at that point the data should own its fields instead.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does one borrowed field often force a lifetime parameter onto the whole struct?
reviewAnswers.answer: A reference is only meaningful relative to the validity of the data it points at, so a struct that stores even one reference must record which external borrow it depends on, and it does that with a lifetime parameter like <'a>. That parameter is not confined to the type definition: it propagates to every function that builds the struct, every struct that contains it as a field, and every return type that hands it back. This is the contagion the chapter warns about — one &'a str field can turn an entire chain of downstream types into Thing<'a>, which is why borrowed fields should be kept local rather than spread through the data model.

reviewAnswers.question: What problem does Box<T> solve that plain owned T does not?
reviewAnswers.answer: Box<T> provides heap indirection while keeping a single owner, which plain owned T cannot do when the type would otherwise need a known, finite size that it does not have. The canonical case is recursion: a struct or enum cannot contain itself by value because its size would be infinite, but boxing the recursive field stores a pointer-sized handle and breaks the cycle. Box also lets you store an unsized or large value behind a fixed-size, movable pointer without involving any reference counting, since there is still exactly one owner.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is Arc<T> not a synonym for 'safe to share and mutate however I want'?
reviewAnswers.answer: Arc<T> makes only the reference count atomic, so it safely answers the question of shared ownership across threads — it does nothing to make the inner value mutable. By itself Arc gives shared read-only access; concurrent mutation through it would be a data race, which the type system prevents by not offering interior mutability. To mutate shared state you must wrap the interior in a synchronization type, such as Arc<Mutex<T>> or Arc<RwLock<T>>. And Arc<T> is only Send and Sync when T itself is thread-safe, so the inner type still has to uphold its own thread-safety guarantees.

reviewAnswers.question: Why do offsets, ranges, or IDs often beat self-references inside owned structs?
reviewAnswers.answer: A self-reference — a field that borrows from another field of the same struct — cannot be expressed in safe Rust, because moving the struct would invalidate the internal pointer and the borrow conflicts with owning the buffer. Storing stable metadata instead, such as a Range<usize> byte offset or a typed token id, sidesteps the problem entirely: the metadata has no lifetime parameter — plain Copy integers like usize offsets, or a cheaply cloned Range<usize> — so the struct stays movable and storable, and the accessor reconstructs a borrowed &str from &self at call time by slicing the owned buffer. The one obligation is to keep that metadata in sync with the buffer, since mutating the buffer can shift positions and make stored offsets stale, just as a raw pointer would dangle.
